extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, psychology, and aesthetics interested in theories of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing normative and descriptive criteria about what counts as humor, why laughter occurs, and how comedy functions — drawing on philosophical, psychological, ethological, and evolutionary accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schopenhauer's Incongruity Account of Laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of laughter is the sudden perception of the incongruity between a concept and the real objects that have been thought through it; laughter is the expression of this incongruity (Book I, sec. 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the convict-card-player and the Austrian walking joke show conceiving an abstract rule and failing to notice an excluded case. Explains offensiveness of being laughed at (announces incongruity between our conceptions and reality) and the pleasure in laughter as perception (perception 'wins' over effortful thought).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kierkegaard: Humor as Contradiction (the Comical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of humor (the 'comical') is a disparity between what is expected and what is experienced; Kierkegaard calls this 'contradiction.' Humor marks a stage of existential awareness (boundary between ethical and religious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes irony and humor (irony between aesthetic and ethical). Comic = painless contradiction; tragic = suffering contradiction. Example: baker who refuses a beggar because 'we cannot give to everybody' (a contradiction that is comical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity Theory (core: violation of mental patterns/expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises when something perceived or thought about violates standard mental patterns and normal expectations — an unexpected or anomalous element produces incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies broadly (including puns and wordplay). Note: repeated exposure can create an expected incongruity yet still be funny in some senses; details of how incongruity yields amusement vary across theorists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-Resolution (Schultz, Suls): enjoyment from resolving incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: What is enjoyed in many kinds of humor is not mere incongruity but the cognitive fitting of an apparently anomalous element into a conceptual schema — 'getting' the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unresolvable incongruity is labeled 'nonsense' rather than humor. Example: Mae West's 'institution' line — pleasure akin to puzzle-solving when the punch line prompts reinterpretation of earlier material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beattie's Caution: Perceiving Incongruity Is Not Sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception of incongruity does not automatically produce laughter; other stronger emotions (fear, pity, moral disapprobation, indignation, disgust) can attend the perception and block risible emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why identical incongruity sometimes produces fear or anger rather than amusement; prompts qualification of any theory that treats incongruity-perception as sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Michael Clark's Three Features for Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Three necessary and sufficient features: (1) A person perceives (thinks, imagines) an object as being incongruous. (2) The person enjoys perceiving (thinking, imagining) the object. (3) The person enjoys the perceived (thought, imagined) incongruity at least partly for itself, rather than solely for some ulterior reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation refines earlier incongruity accounts by adding the requirement of enjoyment and intrinsic appreciation of the incongruity; still may be challenged as not fully specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Humorous Amusement from Other Non-humorous Enjoyments of Incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all enjoyment of violated expectations is humorous; aesthetic categories such as the grotesque, macabre, horrible, bizarre, and fantastic involve non-humorous enjoyment of violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dramatic irony in Oedipus the King allows audiences to 'enjoy' incongruity without it being humorous; refine claims that all incongruity-enjoyment equals humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play Theory: Humor as Play (virtue and social benefit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is a form of play; historically defended by Aristotle and Aquinas as eutrapelia (right-wittedness): play and amusement give rest to the soul and can be virtuous when exercised appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits listed: psychological rest, social lubrication, tolerance for ambiguity and diversity, creative problem-solving, reducing negative emotions in difficult communications. Warnings about excess (buffoonery) or deficiency (boorishness). Example: a humorous debt-collection line showing playful tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethology of Play Signals: Smiling and Laughter as Play Signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Smiling and laughing evolved as play signals (from ape facial/vocal displays) to mark that mock-aggressive behavior is not real aggression; human laughter evolved into 'ha ha ha' on the out-breath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: relaxed open-mouth display, shallow staccato breathing, differences from real aggression facial tension. Explains why laughter is primarily social and why similar behaviors appear in chimps and gorillas during tickling/play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gricean Maxim Violations as Humor Mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often depends on flouting conversational maxims (Grice): do not say what you believe to be false; do not say without evidence; avoid obscurity; avoid ambiguity; be brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking these rules produces specific comic effects: Rule 1 — exaggeration/lying for effect; Rule 2 — presenting fantasies as facts; Rule 3 — vagueness to create humor; Rule 4 — ambiguity exploited in punch lines; Rule 5 — verbosity turned into comic rant. Example: 'I love cats. They taste a lot like chicken.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary Psychology: Sexual Selection Hypothesis for Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor may have been sexually selected: in mate competition, humor signals intelligence, cleverness, adaptability, and a desire to please, making individuals more attractive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites contemporary evolutionary work linking humor production (especially in males) to mating displays; this account helps explain some forms of humor's social functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful Aggression vs Real Hostility: Interpretation and Harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Much humor is playfully aggressive (mock-aggression) and should not be read as literal assertions about target groups; however, such play keeps stereotypes circulating and can be harmful in contexts of prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Polish jokes were popular as fantasies of stupidity rather than expressions of real hostility; nevertheless, repeating stereotypes can perpetuate prejudice. Philosophical mistakes occur when playful jokes are treated as real hostile acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Objectionability Criterion for Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is morally objectionable when it perpetuates harmful stereotypes or treats subjects that should be taken seriously as objects of play, thereby blocking compassion or responsible action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of egregious insensitivity: National Lampoon's 'Dessert Issue' cover parodying a starving child. Use this criterion to evaluate comedic content's ethical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as a Means of Fostering Abstract/Rational Perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor enables a nonpractical, abstract frame of mind: by suspending immediate practical concerns, one can view violations and failures from an objective, depersonalized standpoint that supports rationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate (not in imminent danger), this shift reduces negative emotions and promotes perspective-taking ('see ourselves as other people do'). Counterexample: when immediate action is needed (sulfuric acid), the playful mode is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stress-Reduction and Physiological Benefits of Laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and playful shift reduce stress-related chemicals (epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol), lower heart rate and muscle tension, increase pain tolerance, and boost immune-system activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical and empirical claims invoked to justify humor's value for health; relevant when arguing for practical benefits of humor interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy vs Tragedy: Contrasting Aesthetic and Social Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy treats life's incongruities with pragmatic, anti-heroic responses (deal-making, trickery, fleeing) and valorizes cleverness and adaptability; tragedy valorizes emotional engagement, heroic ideals, and warrior virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal differences: comedy uses common speech, inclusive social focus (family, groups), more character types including lower classes and women; tragedy uses elevated language and centers on heroic individuals. These differences explain distinct moral and social messages of each genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affinities Between Standup Comedy and Philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Standup comedy and philosophy share features: conversational format, reflection on familiar puzzling experiences, question-driven inquiry ('X—what's up with that?'), emotional disengagement, critical thinking, attention to language, and pleasure in novel perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these affinities as evaluative criteria when comparing comedic work to philosophical inquiry or when designing comedy that aspires to philosophical reflection; examples include quips by Russell and collections that pair comedy with philosophy.
